title: low-touch-tool-routing-and-structured-streaming-prd
body:
Overview

This PRD draft proposes a low-friction approach for combining streaming output, explicit tool calling, and opinionated structured output contracts in the Hosted API. The goal is pragmatic: make it straightforward for product teams and third-party SDKs to adopt progressive streaming with tool invocations while keeping backward compatibility, observable failure modes, and simple developer ergonomics.

Problem statement

We regularly hear three related complaints from engineering teams building production LLM features:
- Streaming is powerful but hard to reason about when tool calls, retries, and structured payloads are mixed in.
- SDK ergonomics are inconsistent across languages; integrating tool-level back-and-forth often forces complex client-side state machines.
- Observability for streamed tool workflows is fragmented: token telemetry, tool latency, and structured-output validation are scattered across traces.

Non-goals

- This PRD does not propose a new tool execution runtime (we will rely on the existing task runners).
- It does not attempt to replace the function-calling surface, but to provide a compatible streaming contract and SDK patterns.

Key principles

1) Low-touch: defaults should work for the median developer with minimal plumbing. SDKs should offer a single async iterator or callback API that yields enriched frames.
2) Contract-first structured output: encourage predictable typed payloads with light validation so downstream integrations can be deterministic.
3) Progressive delivery: allow partial structured results and incremental tool responses rather than enforcing all-or-nothing commits.
4) Observable fallbacks: every crossing from model -> tool -> model must be traceable with clear metrics.

User stories

- As a frontend engineer I want the page to render partial answers as the model streams, and then replace or augment them when a tool returns authoritative data.
- As an integrator I want to call a tool from the model and surface the tool's streamed progress to users (e.g., file download progress) without writing a bespoke state machine.
- As an SRE I want to know when tool-calls increase latency or cause model fallback so we can tune routing/policy.

Proposed surface and behaviors

1) Frame-based streaming envelope
- Each stream is composed of newline-delimited frames. Each frame describes a logical event: prompt token, partial-structured, tool-request, tool-response-chunk, tool-end, final-structured, error, heartbeat.
- Frames are text-first for backwards compatibility; structured frames contain a typed payload field with a lightweight schema identifier.
- Example frame sequence (pseudo-syntax):
  <<init>> { type: init, session: sess-ABC, schema: structured-v1 }
  <<token>> { text: We recommend }
  <<partial_structured>> { schema: order-v1, payload: { line_items: [ { sku: 123 } ] } }
  <<tool_request>> { name: payments.charge, args_schema: payments-v1, hint: requires-3ds }
  <<tool_response_chunk>> { chunk_index: 0, progress: 12% }
  <<tool_end>> { status: success }
  <<final_structured>> { schema: order-v1, payload: { id: ORD-45, total: 17.50 } }
  <<done>> { }

2) Tool calling handshake (stream-friendly)
- The model may emit a tool_request frame in-stream, which instructs the client to invoke an external tool and stream back responses with tool_response_chunk frames.
- Clients MUST acknowledge the tool_request by emitting a tool_ack frame in the same session stream if the client intends to run the tool; otherwise a tool_reject frame with reason should be sent.
- If the client runs the tool asynchronously, it can interleave progress frames back into the stream. The server will maintain ordering and track outstanding tool calls per session.
- Timeouts and cancellations are explicit: tool_cancel frames can be sent by either side.

3) Structured output conventions
- We define a small registry of common schema ids (structured-v1, order-v1, toolcall-v1). Schemas are optional but recommended for critical integrations.
- Validation is best-effort server-side with warning metadata included in frames rather than rejecting the stream. This preserves UX for partial results while letting teams catch regressions.
- Final structured frames carry a signature blob (hash of canonical serialization) to help clients differentiate model-supplied vs tool-verified values.

4) SDK ergonomics patterns (recommended defaults)
- Primary call shape: an async iterator that yields Frame objects. Example usage (pseudo):
  for frame in client.streamCompletion(req):
    if frame.type == token: renderToken(frame.text)
    if frame.type == partial_structured: mergePartial(frame.schema, frame.payload)
    if frame.type == tool_request: // SDK helper pauses model stream, triggers tool adapter
      runToolAndPushChunks(frame.name, frame.args)
- Provide a simple adapter for tool execution: runToolAndPushChunks(name, args) which handles ack/reject and emits chunks back to the session with backpressure handling.
- Language SDKs must include a "no-op" adapter default that returns immediate tool_reject when a tool is not configured; this keeps behaviour predictable.
- Expose typed Frame objects rather than raw strings to reduce parsing code across clients. Include a minimal runtime for schema validation.

5) Backward compatibility and fallbacks
- If a client does not understand structured frames, frames degrade to plain token text plus a small summary token: e.g., token text contains "[tool-request:payments.charge]" so legacy clients still surface intent.
- Server will allow toggling strict_validation in customer config; default is permissive.

Observability and telemetry

Essential metrics to capture per session & per route:
- token_latency_p50/p95, token_throughput, frames_per_session
- tool_request_count, tool_latency_p50/p95, tool_success_rate, tool_chunks_per_request
- structured_validation_warnings, schema_mismatch_rate
- SDK-level: ack_time_median (time client takes to ack a tool_request), tool_backpressure_events

Trace model: every frame includes a trace_id and optional parent_tool_id so we can reconstruct full causal chains. Events should map to datapoints in Console (per-route). Alerts: elevated tool latency or high schema_mismatch_rate should trigger an incident playbook.

Rollout plan

Phase 0: internal beta with product teams and Solutions Engineering. Enable structured-v1 and handshake flows behind a feature flag. Collect telemetry and iterate frame shapes.
Phase 1: public beta as opt-in on new routes. SDK shipped with helpers and no-op adapter. Provide migration guide for teams using function-calling.
Phase 2: default enablement for new customers, with opt-out for existing. Add stricter validation options as enterprise feature.

Success metrics

- Time-to-first-meaningful-paint for streaming UI down 20% for adoptors.
- Tool-invocation integration time for customers reduced from weeks to days (survey metric).
- Decrease in ambiguous fallback incidents where UI shows inaccurate data by 50%.

Open questions and risks

- Schema proliferation: how to curate and version schemas across customers? Proposal: host an internal schema registry in Console and require schema ids to include semantic version.
- Tool security posture: streaming tool responses could leak secrets if not sanitized. Risk mitigations: require tool adapters to run under managed runtime with policy enforcement for PII detection.
- Client complexity: while the intent is low-touch defaults, advanced integrations will need fine-grained control; we must avoid SDK bloat.

Appendix: example session narrative

Client opens stream with role: user, schema_hint: structured-v1. Model starts streaming an explanation. At frame 3 the model emits tool_request: payments.charge with args schema. SDK auto-acknowledges because customer has payments adapter enabled. The client runs the adapter which streams progress (tool_response_chunk progress 0..100). The server forwards these chunks into the same session and the model picks up the final tool_end and emits final_structured with order id. The UI shows progressive answers, then a payment status bar, then an order confirmation card populated from final_structured. Console shows a single trace with three spans: model-stream, tool-exec (with chunk metrics), model-finalize.

Appendix: minimal example SDK shipping checklist

- Frame parser that returns typed Frame objects
- Async iterator / callback API consistent across languages
- Tool adapter shim with ack/reject defaults and backpressure support
- Built-in lightweight schema validator and warning emitter
- Example integration: payments and search adapters

Next steps

- Align with serving-runtime on maximum frame rate and streaming resource accounting.
- Prototype the SDK iterator + tool-adapter in TypeScript and Python.
- Run internal hackathon with Solutions Engineering to recreate 3 example integrations (payments, search-with-snippet, file-processing) and gather UX notes.

Notes to reviewers

- Focus feedback on the frame envelope shape and the required fields for tool_request/tool_response_chunk. The handshake semantics are intentionally minimal to keep SDKs small.
- Call out any security/regulatory concerns early; these will affect how we store tool logs and telemetry in Console.
